examples.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t) =\cos(2t+1),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u= 2t +1.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d t} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d t = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t) =4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t=\int 4\text{d}t=4t+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1},\,4t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨1,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨1,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\,\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.
